A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same POMG policy-regret research. Their complete main texts, equations and appendices are readable, allowing relocated proofs to be matched and substantive additions to be distinguished from renumbering.

before.justification: V1 contains theoretical algorithms, bounds, proofs and analytical hard instances, but no original experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes in either the main text or Appendices A-H.

after.justification: Appendix I reports original bandit-embedded POMG simulations and a digits-based adaptive-adversary experiment, including numerical findings, multiple seeds and uncertainty bands in Figures 3-6.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes from fixed geometrically growing epochs to geometrically capped epochs with per-episode MLE recomputation and likelihood-based early termination. Confidence construction also changes through data-dependent discretization, revised failure-budget allocation and an mB0 floor. These changes alter execution and policy selection.

E1.justification: V1 has no empirical evaluation coverage. Appendix I adds evaluations on bandit-embedded POMG instances and a classification environment derived from 1,797 scikit-learn digits images, with coarse observations and an adaptive class-distribution adversary.

E2.justification: V2 introduces actual empirical comparators: the fixed-schedule algorithm without termination in Experiment 1, and fixed schedule, epsilon-greedy and uniform play in Experiment 3. V1 contains no evaluated baseline comparisons; the theoretical literature comparisons are separate.

E3.justification: Appendix I introduces expected-value policy-regret measurement, horizon sweeps with changing instance sizes or shrinking gaps, arm-count and memory sweeps, and a 16,384-episode digits protocol. The latter specifies PCA quantization, six fixed classifiers and a memory-4 adversary. These are new protocols, not revisions of existing experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds a controlled termination-test ablation and analyses of regret scaling, deployment counts, dimension dependence and warm-up costs as memory varies. Figures 3-4 provide empirical evidence for these questions, which were not experimentally investigated in v1.

E5.justification: V2 introduces repeated-run uncertainty reporting across its empirical suite: 20 independent seeds for Experiments 1-2 and 10 for Experiment 3. Curves report means with bands of plus or minus two standard errors, explicitly described as approximate 95% confidence bands. V1 has no empirical run or error-bar reporting.

E6.justification: New results include average regret 0.250 versus 0.100 for fixed versus terminated epochs at T=2^15, and a horizon-scaling slope of 0.53. Figure 6 reports digits cumulative regret of approximately 207, 1844, 987 and 4097 for termination, fixed schedule, epsilon-greedy and uniform play at T=2^14. V1 reports no corresponding empirical outcomes.

T1.justification: V2 redefines dE through separate channel-error classes, adds the sign-witness Eluder proof in Appendix C, and strengthens structural/statistical assumptions. Proposition D.5 supplies a fixed-schedule counterexample; capped summability and switch-count proofs replace v1's uncapped argument. Main, fading-memory and tabular bounds are substantively revised, including confidence-radius and memory dependence.

C1.justification: The sqrt(T) headline remains, but v2 replaces the claim that fixed geometric epochs and O(log T) deployments suffice with a guarantee for statistically terminated epochs. Sections 1.1 and 6 add the necessity of data-dependent switching as a contribution. The claimed guarantee also uses a redefined complexity parameter and revised assumptions.

C2.justification: V1 explains success through logarithmic policy-transport costs; v2 explains why transport does not enter its main bound and why additional terminations are affordable. It qualifies finite-window and coordinate-structured applicability, recasts fading-memory optimality as an open question (F.1 to G.1), and adds limitations concerning simulated adversaries and tractable oracle implementations.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's theoretical pseudocode, Appendix I documents clipped Bernoulli MLE, KL-confidence computation by bisection, practical thresholds, classifier construction and adversary parameters. It reports a few CPU minutes for the suite and provides a link where code, a notebook and exact seeds are stated to be available; that external availability was not verified.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning around predictive-state learning, POMG posterior sampling and low-switching RL, including Bai et al. (2019), Qiao et al. (2022) and Qiu et al. (2023). The concurrent-work comparison adds distinctions concerning private adversary histories and credits an impossibility result, beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The contributions, algorithm rationale, proof exposition and related-work narrative undergo substantial rewriting. The causal-decomposition and complexity sections exchange order, the main proof sketch is condensed with an extended version in Appendix D.1, and the appendices gain a roadmap and reorganized proof subsections.

P2.justification: V1 has no numbered figures or tables. V2 adds two tables comparing guarantees and summarizing results, causal-decomposition and epoch diagrams in Figures 1-2, and experimental plots and data visualizations in Figures 3-6. These substantially expand the paper's visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses a central validity problem: Proposition D.5 shows that v1's fixed schedule can incur linear regret, while the revised algorithm and capped-error/switch-count proofs directly address that failure. Explicit complexity derivations, clearer qualifications and multi-seed experiments substantially strengthen support and transparency. Stronger assumptions, per-episode MLE computation and simplified simulated experiments limit scope, but do not outweigh this central correction.
